tax1-render-unto-caesar.reason: Opens on the Matthew 22 trap; the two errors (resentment, substitution) that answer the title arrive only near the end, and the lesson closes on a question rather than the answer.
tax1-render-unto-caesar.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Are you paying the taxman well and leaving Yahweh the leftovers? Many careful households are. Jesus named two real claims in one breath (Matthew 22:21): the coin, stamped with Caesar's image, goes to Caesar; the person, made in Yahweh's image, goes to Yahweh, and that claim is far larger. Paying the first with real care while the second gets whatever is left is the more respectable error and the more serious one. Here is how the passage shows it.
tax1-render-unto-caesar.example: TWO COLUMNS, ONE HOUSEHOLD. Say a family keeps a filing cabinet for the tax return, pays a preparer, and has every date on the calendar. That is the left column, and it is done well. Now look at the right column, what is owed to Yahweh. No folder, no date, no figure, because nobody mails an invoice for it. Whatever was left in December went there. Nobody in that house resents the tax, and nobody meant to shortchange Him. The order of care simply ran backwards.
tax1-render-unto-caesar.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Are you paying the taxman well and leaving Yahweh the leftovers? The coin answers it. Render to Caesar what bears his mark, honestly and without resentment, because Jesus held the coin and said render. Then give the larger claim the better treatment, because you bear Yahweh's image and belong to Him. Write both columns, ask which one got the professional care this year, and let the answer change the order. The leftovers were never His portion; the first and best were.

teen.open: Are you careful with what you owe the government and careless with what you owe Yahweh? Jesus said both claims are real, and His is the bigger one.
teen.close: So pay your taxes honestly, no grumbling. But do not give Yahweh what is left over. You carry His image. He gets your first and best.

senior.open: The title asks whether we have been diligent with the tax and casual with what belongs to Yahweh. Jesus named two real claims, and the one on the person who bears His image is by far the greater.
senior.close: The answer the coin gives is plain. Render the tax faithfully, without resentment, and then give Yahweh's column the care that the civil column has been getting, rather than whatever remains at the end of the year.

tax2-then-are-the-children-free.reason: The answer (two separate decisions: do I owe it, and do I insist) arrives mid-lesson after the narrative; it ends on the exercise, mostly landing it but not naming why winning feels like losing.
tax2-then-are-the-children-free.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why can winning the point feel like losing? Because every disputed obligation holds two separate decisions. The first is fact and law: do I owe this? The second is judgment: since I do not, should I insist? When you let the first answer the second, you can be right the whole time and still spend credibility, a relationship or a testimony to collect money you would never have missed. Jesus made both decisions, on purpose, in Matthew 17.
tax2-then-are-the-children-free.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why does winning the point feel like losing? Because the point was only decision one. Jesus answered it plainly, the children are free, and never took it back. Then He made decision two on its own: notwithstanding, lest we offend them. He paid from a separate provision, so nobody else bore the cost, for a named reason. Do the same. Get the first answer right, then decide the second on purpose. Being right will no longer cost you what money cannot buy back.

teen.open: Ever win an argument and still feel like you lost? There are two questions hiding in every dispute: am I right, and should I push it?
teen.close: Jesus was right and said so. Then He chose not to push it, for a clear reason. Answer both questions on purpose, and being right stops costing you friends.

senior.open: Being right and being wise about it are two different decisions, and the trouble comes when we let the first one make the second for us. Matthew 17 shows Jesus making them separately.
senior.close: So the feeling of loss has a cause. The exemption was real and Jesus stated it, yet He chose not to insist, paid from a separate provision, and gave His reason. Make your second decision deliberately, and your rightness will stop costing you in every currency that is not money.

tax3-all-the-world-should-be-taxed.reason: The title's how (record machinery is not outside Yahweh's government; keep your books as service) emerges only in the second half and is scattered; it ends on a limit, not the answer.
tax3-all-the-world-should-be-taxed.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How does Yahweh use the records you resent? Luke 2 shows the pattern. An emperor's tax decree required every man to register in his family's town, and that filing requirement carried Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem. Nobody doing the paperwork knew. The point is not that every form hides a secret blessing. It is that record and revenue are not outside Yahweh's government. So your own records can be kept as service, not resented as a levy.
tax3-all-the-world-should-be-taxed.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How does Yahweh use the records you resent? He is not hindered by the machinery of record, nor absent from it; in Bethlehem He used a tax filing as His instrument while the clerks just wrote names. Your part is smaller and sturdier. Name the record you resent, write down what it has already given you, and keep it this year as service. It will not make the filing interesting. It will keep the record that the hard year will need.

teen.open: Jesus was born in Bethlehem because of a tax form. Yahweh was not stopped by paperwork; He used it.
teen.close: You do not have to love keeping records. But they are not outside Yahweh's reach. Keep them as service, and they will be there when you need them.

senior.open: Luke records that a tax registration brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem. The lesson is not that every form is secretly a blessing, but that record-keeping is never outside Yahweh's government.
senior.close: So the records we resent are not wasted labour. Yahweh once used such paperwork as His instrument; we can keep ours as service, and they will be ready in the year that tests them.

tax4-the-rich-shall-not-give-more.reason: Says early that structure beats amount, but the plain answer (no; knowability, equality both ways, stated use) is only stated two-thirds in; ends near it but on a household finding, not the answer.
tax4-the-rich-shall-not-give-more.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Is a levy fair because of its rate? No. The rate is the least telling number. The half-shekel of Exodus 30 shows three better questions. Can the payer state the amount and the method in one sentence? Is the same rule applied to everyone, so the poor are not shut out and the rich cannot buy extra standing? Is the use named in the law itself? Here is how the text sets each one.
tax4-the-rich-shall-not-give-more.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is a levy fair because of its rate? Exodus 30 says look elsewhere. The half-shekel was knowable, with its own conversion written in. It was equal in both directions: the rich shall not give more, and the poor shall not give less. Its use was named where the duty was named. A small charge nobody can explain, applied unevenly, going nowhere named, is worse than a larger one that passes all three. Ask the three questions, and you will judge a levy truly.

teen.open: Is a tax fair just because the rate is low? The Bible's first census payment says to ask three other questions instead.
teen.close: Can you explain it in one sentence? Does everyone pay by the same rule? Do you know where it goes? Those three matter more than the rate.

senior.open: We usually judge a levy by its rate. The half-shekel of Exodus 30 points to three questions that matter more: is it knowable, is it equal in both directions, and is its use stated?
senior.close: So the rate alone does not make a levy just. One that can be stated plainly, applies the same rule to rich and poor alike, and names its purpose is the sounder arrangement, whatever its size.

tax5-he-will-take-the-tenth.reason: The why (hearing a cost is not accounting for it; nobody ever saw the total) arrives in the middle after the 1 Samuel list; ends on a second column and a pointer to later sessions.
tax5-he-will-take-the-tenth.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. The price was read aloud, so why did the bill still shock them? Because hearing a cost and accounting for it are two different things. Samuel told Israel every item in advance, and they consented. But they never set the items down as one total and weighed it. Most property owners live the same way: every notice read, the sum never added. The remedy is an itemised schedule with a total at the bottom.
tax5-he-will-take-the-tenth.example: ONE PAGE, ONE TOTAL. Say a household writes it out for the first time. Property tax, $3,400. Association fee, $1,800. Required insurance, $2,100. Inspections, licences and filing fees, $300. Each figure arrived on its own notice, and each notice was read. Added together, the line at the bottom says $7,600 a year. Nothing on the page is new information. The total is. Then a second column marks which items they chose knowingly and which were added to them after they bought.
tax5-he-will-take-the-tenth.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why did the bill still shock them? Israel had full disclosure and informed consent, and the grief still came exactly as Samuel described, because they were informed but never accounted. The cure is not more information. It is the total. Write every tax, levy, fee, mandated insurance and inspection with a real figure, add them, and mark which you consented to and which were added later. Then the cost has been weighed, not just heard, and the bill will not surprise you.

teen.open: Israel was told exactly what a king would cost, and it still hurt. Why? Hearing the price is not the same as adding it up.
teen.close: So add it up. Write every cost on one page with a total. Once you have seen the real number, the bill will not catch you off guard.

senior.open: Samuel read Israel the full cost of a king before they agreed, yet they still cried out later. The reason is that hearing each cost is not the same as having accounted for the whole.
senior.close: The remedy is an itemised schedule with a total, and a second column separating what you consented to from what was added afterwards. The total, once weighed, is what turns disclosure into real knowledge.

tax6-they-sought-their-register.reason: The principle (a right you cannot document cannot be used when tested; produce it in ten minutes) sits mid-lesson; the lesson ends on two open questions rather than the answer.
tax6-they-sought-their-register.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Would your claims survive a test? Being right in your heart is not enough. In Ezra 2 some families were likely exactly who they said they were, but their register could not be found, so they were set aside. A right you cannot document cannot be used on the day it is tested. The drill shows you which: produce each key document from where you keep it, inside ten minutes.
tax6-they-sought-their-register.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Would your claims survive a test? Only the ones you can produce. The families in Ezra 2 were not accused of lying; their register simply was not found, and their standing was suspended until it could be settled. So run the drill now: the deed, the survey, the easement, the cost basis, the lien release, each from its real place, inside ten minutes. Whatever fails tonight, with nothing at stake, you can fix before the day it would cost you.

teen.open: Knowing something is yours is not the same as proving it. In Ezra 2, people lost their place because a record could not be found.
teen.close: So find your important papers now. If you can show them in ten minutes, your claim is ready. If not, fix it today while nothing is riding on it.

senior.open: Ezra 2 records families who were very likely who they claimed to be, yet could not show their register. The lesson is that moral entitlement and provable entitlement can come apart.
senior.close: Your claims are ready only when the document can be produced, from where you keep it, within minutes. A failure found in a quiet drill is a mercy; the same failure found under a real challenge is costly.

tax7-restore-it-in-the-principal-and-add.reason: Opens promising a remedy but states it only after the verse setup; the why of the twenty percent is mid-lesson, and the ending turns to the exercise and Zacchaeus rather than restating the answer.
tax7-restore-it-in-the-principal-and-add.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. You found the error yourself; what now? Leviticus 6:5 gives three parts. Restore the principal, the full value. Add a fifth part more, twenty percent. Give it to the person it belongs to, not to a cause. The extra fifth matters because simply returning what was taken leaves the injured man behind and the offender ahead, having had free use of what was not his. The fifth makes the correction real.
tax7-restore-it-in-the-principal-and-add.example: FOUR HUNDRED DOLLARS, DONE RIGHT. Take the lesson's own case: you took four hundred dollars from one neighbour. The principal is $400. The fifth part is $80. So $480 goes to that neighbour, by name, with the conversation it requires. Giving $600 to a good work instead may be admirable, but it is not this statute. The neighbour is still where he was, and the debt is still unpaid.
tax7-restore-it-in-the-principal-and-add.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What does Leviticus 6 say to do with an error you found yourself? Restore the principal, add the fifth, and give it to the one it belongs to, on the same day you come to Yahweh about it. The twenty percent is not severity; it is the arithmetic that makes being wrong cost the one who was wrong, instead of the one who was wronged. It will cost more than silence. That cost is the statute working, and it settles what silence never could.

teen.open: Found a mistake that went your way? Leviticus 6 says give it back, add twenty percent, and give it to the person you owe.
teen.close: Just paying back the exact amount still leaves them behind. The extra twenty percent makes it right. And it goes to them, not to some other good cause.

senior.open: Leviticus 6 is the statute for the day you find your own error. It names the remedy: the principal, a fifth part more, and payment to the very person who was wronged.
senior.close: The fifth part is what turns stopping the wrong into actually righting it, and paying the true party closes the door on substituting general generosity for a specific debt. It costs more than silence, and it is meant to.

tax8-will-a-man-rob-god.reason: The answer (with no bill, the obligation drifts unnoticed, as in Malachi 3:8) is reached mid-lesson after recapping the course; ends on setting a deadline, which lands it only partly.
tax8-will-a-man-rob-god.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. What happens when nobody sends the bill? The obligation drifts. Every other duty in this course has someone outside the house who notices a shortfall. What is owed to Yahweh has no notice, no late fee and no examiner, so it slips without anyone choosing it. That is how a whole nation in Malachi 3 robbed Him and sincerely asked how. The remedy is to give that column a figure.
tax8-will-a-man-rob-god.example: TWO NUMBERS ON ONE PAGE. Say a household has always assumed its giving was about where it should be. This year they finally write two figures side by side: $60,000 came in, $2,400 went to Him. The actual ratio is four percent, not the one they had in their heads. Nobody decided that. No one was careless on purpose. It simply happened in the space where a number should have been, which is the very drift Malachi describes.
tax8-will-a-man-rob-god.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. What happens when nobody sends the bill? It drifts, in honourable homes as much as careless ones, until the charge arrives as news. So be your own notice. Write what came in and what went to Him, see the true ratio, and decide next year in writing before it starts. This is the one account Yahweh invites you to test by obedience, not inspection (Malachi 3:10). Every other bill brings its own deadline. This one has only the one you set, so set it.

teen.open: Nobody sends you a bill for what you owe Yahweh. So what happens? It quietly slips, without you ever deciding to let it.
teen.close: Be your own reminder. Write down what came in and what you gave. Set your plan before the year starts. Yahweh says test Him by doing it.

senior.open: Every other obligation has an outside party who notices when it is short. What is owed to Yahweh has none, and Malachi 3 shows what follows: a sincere people who had drifted without knowing.
senior.close: So the safeguard is a figure. Set what came in beside what went to Him, see the actual ratio, and decide the coming year in writing. It is the one account He asks to be proved by obedience.
